# Prompt

# Vizmatic agent prompt

Use Vizmatic to explain things visually from code. It makes two kinds of output:

- A **film** is motion. Write a TypeScript function with `vizmatic/stage`. It plays live in a browser and exports to MP4, WebM, GIF, PNG, and SVG.
- A **figure** is a still. Write TSX with typed components from `vizmatic`. It renders to PNG and SVG in dark and light themes.

Vizmatic requires Node.js 20 or newer. MP4 and WebM also need FFmpeg.

```bash
npm install vizmatic
```

For pnpm 11, allow esbuild's install script with `allowBuilds: { esbuild: true }` in the root `pnpm-workspace.yaml`.

## Films

Start from a template, or write the function yourself. Templates are `explainer`, `equation`, `architecture`, `chart`, and `deck`.

```bash
npx vizmatic new intro --template explainer
```

```ts
import { axes, draw, dynamic, dot, fadeIn, film, line, tex, write } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ title: 'A limit you can see' }, (s) => {
    s.chapter('The curve')
    const plot = s.add(axes({ x: [-1, 4], y: [-1, 9], grid: true, width: 1080, height: 660 }).at(-340, 60))
    s.play(draw(plot.grid, { lag: 0.02 }), draw(plot.lines), fadeIn(plot.numbers))
    s.play(draw(plot.plot((x) => x * x, { stroke: 'blue', width: 5 })))

    s.chapter('The secant')
    const h = s.value(2)
    const secant = s.add(dynamic(() => {
        const slope = 2 + h.value
        return [
            line(plot.world(0.2, 1 + slope * -0.8), plot.world(3.2, 1 + slope * 2.2), { stroke: 'yellow', width: 3.5 }),
            dot(9, 'yellow').at(plot.world(1 + h.value, (1 + h.value) ** 2)),
        ]
    }))
    s.play(fadeIn(secant))
    s.play(write(s.add(tex('m = 2 + h', { size: 64 }).at(600, -120))))
    s.play(h.to(0.02, { duration: 4 }))
    s.wait(1.5)
})
```

Rules of the engine:

- The stage is 1920 by 1080. (0, 0) is the center and y points down. Plots convert with `plot.world(x, y)`.
- The build function runs once and may run again while assets load. Keep it free of side effects.
- `s.play(...)` writes animation and moves time forward. `s.wait(seconds)` holds. `s.at(time, build)` authors at another time.
- A `dynamic(() => ...)` drawing rebuilds on every frame. Read `value.value` inside it to drive anything.
- `morph(a, b)` leaves `b` on stage and `a` hidden. Later code refers to `b`.
- A `duration` on `s.play` stretches every animation to fill it, and a `duration` inside one of those animations has no effect. For different lengths, leave it off `s.play`, set it on each animation, and use `delay` for an offset: `s.play(fadeOut(oldText, { duration: 0.15 }), delay(fadeIn(newText, { duration: 0.25 }), 0.1))`. Inside a `s.play` that has a duration, use `seq(fadeOut(oldText), fadeIn(newText))`.
- Use `font: 'text-serif'` for sentences, labels, and numbers. Use `font: 'serif'` only for short titles at a large size.
- Colors are look tokens such as `'blue'`, `'yellow'`, `'ink'`, and `'dim'`, so a film renders in every look.
- Run `vizmatic objects` and `vizmatic looks` to see what the installed version offers.

### Check, look, and export

An agent cannot watch a video, so judge a film from the check and from stills.

```bash
npx vizmatic check intro.ts --json
npx vizmatic film intro.ts --frame 3,6.5,12 --width 1280 --out stills
npx vizmatic film intro.ts --out dist/films --look midnight,paper --quality high
```

`vizmatic check` samples the moments where the film comes to rest. It reports `film.off_canvas`, `film.text_overlap`, `film.text_crossed`, and `film.missing_glyph`, each with times, a `box` in canvas pixels, and a `stage` center in authoring coordinates. Fix every error, then open the stills and look at them. `vizmatic preview intro.ts` opens a live player with a timeline for a person to review. The [Studio](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/studio.html) is a visual film editor in the browser for a person who wants to edit by hand.

The check does not look at motion, so a crossfade where two sentences overlap and a blank gap between two pictures both pass it. Add `--motion` to inspect every frame: `npx vizmatic check intro.ts --motion --json`. It reports a problem that appears only in motion as a warning, and 0.2 seconds or more with nothing visible as `film.blank`. Judge each warning, because the check cannot tell a collision from one picture that replaces another. `--content-top <px>` sets where the content starts, so that a heading that stays up does not hide a blank.

`--audio narration.wav` adds sound, padded or trimmed to the film's length, so hold until the voice ends. `s.caption(text, seconds)` writes a WebVTT file beside the video and draws nothing into the picture. MP4 output is H.264 with settings that QuickTime can play. To join a clip to a film without encoding it again, encode the clip with `filmEncoderSettings(quality)` from `vizmatic/stage/export`.

Motion guidance:

- Use one idea per beat. Hold for a second after each reveal, so a viewer can read it.
- Move the thing being explained. Avoid decorative motion.
- Give color a meaning and keep it. A quantity keeps its color from its first appearance to its last.
- Use chapters. They mark the player's timeline and are the steps of a presentation.

### Lessons

When a film must teach a topic, [lessons.md](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/references/lessons.md) has the full method. In short:

- Put accuracy first, then completeness, clarity, and brevity. There is no target length, so keep every passage that teaches.
- Finish the script before the film. Teach the problem, then the mechanism, then the limits. Keep one worked example throughout.
- Compute every number in the film, and check it with `assert`. The voice and the screen use the same values and the same rounding.
- Keep each title true for as long as it is visible. List every text block with its visible times, and read each one against the picture and the voice.
- Change pictures cleanly. Old text drops under about 25% opacity before new text reaches it, and something stays on screen through the change.
- A person must watch the film at full speed with sound before it is published. You cannot do this, so say that it has not happened.
- Use the computed states from `vizmatic` where they fit: `weightedVectorState`, `categoricalSampling`, `planTeachingRoutedTransfer`, `byteDifferenceState`, and `tokenHistoryState`. Show the limits of each. `check` and `film` accept this import, and `preview` refuses it because it runs in the browser. A project with a checked canvas host can use the same constructions through `createTeachingCanvas(painter)`.

Read a finished film before you write a similar one. `examples/films/` in the package holds them with full source, and the [Films](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/films.html) page plays them.

## Figures

Create `frame.tsx`. `Scene` title and subtitle are optional.

```tsx
<Scene title="Checkout, read path">
  <Flow
    stages={[
      { title: "Gateway", subtitle: "Envoy, p99 9 ms", tone: "blue" },
      { title: "Cart", subtitle: "Go, 840 rps", tone: "purple" },
      { title: "Orders DB", subtitle: "Postgres, primary + 3", tone: "green" },
    ]}
  />
</Scene>
```

```bash
npx vizmatic check ./frame.tsx --theme dark,light --json
npx vizmatic ./frame.tsx --out ./figures --theme dark,light --format both
```

Fix all errors before the final render. Warnings report low contrast, small text, overlapping labels, uneven panel whitespace, connector congestion, and asset fallbacks.

Figures default to the `dense` density, like a figure in an engineering paper. Fill the space with useful detail: runtimes, rates, schemas, and limits. Do not spread three boxes across a slide. Use `density="presentation"` on a `Scene`, or `density` in a render option, only for a room. The densities are `dense`, `compact`, `comfortable`, `presentation`, or a number.

Choose by meaning: `GraphDiagram` for systems, `SequenceDiagram` for interactions, `DataflowDiagram` for lineage, `DeploymentDiagram` for placement and trust, `TransformerTopology` for models, and `LineChart`, `BarChart`, `DataTable`, or `Heatmap` for data. Omit `width` and `height` to auto-grow from 960 by 540.

PNG and SVG output is alpha-transparent by default. Add `--background theme` or `background={c.bg}` for an opaque canvas. Use `preset = "engineering";` with `--theme light` for flat article figures.

Use a full module when a frame needs helper code or data:

```tsx
import { Flow, Scene, getThemeColors, type ThemeMode } from "vizmatic"

export const width = 1040
export const height = 560

export function create(theme: ThemeMode = "dark") {
  const c = getThemeColors(theme)
  return <Scene c={c} title="Runtime path"><Flow c={c} stages={[{ title: "Input", tone: "blue" }, { title: "Check", tone: "purple" }]} /></Scene>
}
```

## Reference

- [CLI](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/docs/cli.html) and [Exporting](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/docs/exporting.html): every flag.
- [Animations](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/docs/animations.html), [Objects](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/docs/objects.html), [Camera](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/docs/camera.html), and [3D](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/docs/three-d.html): the film API.
- [Figure recipes](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/docs/figure-recipes.html) and [Figures reference](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/docs/figures.html): component props and complete frames.
- [Science guide](https://github.com/bvolpato/vizmatic/blob/main/SCIENCE.md): accurate diagrams for math, physics, chemistry, and machine learning.
- [`llms-full.txt`](https://bvolpato.github.io/vizmatic/llms-full.txt): this prompt, all guides, and the component catalog.

## Final response

After creating a visual, report:

- files created or changed
- the exact render command used
- output paths
- which looks or themes rendered
- whether `vizmatic check` passed
- any overflow or layout fixes made
- for a film, which stills you opened, and whether you scanned the motion
- anything you could not verify, including that nobody has watched the film with sound

# Guide: For agents

## A loop that works

An agent cannot watch a video, so the loop relies on checks and stills.

1. Write the film as a TypeScript file.
2. Run `vizmatic check --json` and fix what it reports.
3. Render stills with `--frame` at the moments that matter, and look at them.
4. Export the MP4 when the stills are right.

```bash
npx vizmatic check intro.ts --json
npx vizmatic film intro.ts --frame 2,6,12 --width 1280 --out ./stills
npx vizmatic film intro.ts --quality high --out ./out
```

The check inspects moments of rest. It misses a crossfade where two sentences overlap and a blank gap between two pictures. Add `--motion` to inspect every frame, and judge each warning that it reports. Then extract frames from the MP4 around each change of picture, and read them.

## Films that teach

A lesson needs more than a clean check. [The lesson reference](../references/lessons.md) covers the plan, computed numbers, narration, changes of picture, a frame scan, delivery, and review. An agent cannot judge a lesson at full speed, so a person must watch it with sound before it is published.

[Finished films](../films.html) show the full source for each topic. The package includes them in `examples/films/`.

The package also computes some mechanisms for you, with helpers such as `weightedVectorState` and `tokenHistoryState`. A film can import them from `vizmatic` for `check` and `film`, but `preview` refuses that import because it runs in the browser. [The canvas guide](tsx-animation.html) covers the same constructions for a checked canvas host.

## Install the skill

The portable skill teaches an agent the workflow and the API. See the [agent page](../agents.html) for plugin installs.

```bash
npx skills add bvolpato/vizmatic --skill vizmatic -g -y
```

`vizmatic objects --json` and `vizmatic looks --json` list what is available in the installed version.

## Why the source suits an agent

- A film is one function, with no framework state to hold in mind.
- Layout helpers such as `nextTo`, `alignTo`, and `arrange` replace hand-tuned coordinates.
- Color names come from the look, so an agent does not choose hex values.
- `checkFilm` is also a function, so a test can fail when a label leaves the frame.

```ts
import { checkFilm, film, text } from 'vizmatic/stage'

const draft = film((s) => {
    s.add(text('A title that is much too wide for this frame', { size: 300 }))
    s.wait(1)
})

export async function report(): Promise<string[]> {
    const result = await checkFilm(draft)
    return result.diagnostics.map((item) => `${item.code} at ${item.time.toFixed(1)} s: ${item.message}`)
}
```

# Guide: Animations

Each animation takes optional `duration` and `ease` settings. Without them it uses a length that suits it and the `smooth` ease.

A `duration` on `s.play` stretches every animation in that call to fill it, and it overrides a `duration` set on any of them. To give animations different lengths, leave it off `s.play`.

## Reveal

### draw

`draw` traces strokes in order. Filled shapes outline first and then fill.

```film paired label="A circle and an arrow draw themselves"
import { arrow, circle, draw, film } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const ring = circle(300, { stroke: 'blue', width: 10 }).at(-300, 0)
    const pointer = arrow([100, 220], [750, -220], { stroke: 'yellow', width: 12, tip: 60 })
    s.play(draw(ring), draw(pointer), { duration: 1.6 })
    s.wait(1)
})
```

### write

`write` handwrites text and equations. Each glyph is outlined and then filled, with a small lag between glyphs.

```film paired label="An equation handwrites itself"
import { film, tex, write } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const eq = s.add(tex('e^{i\\pi} + 1 = 0', { size: 190 }))
    s.play(write(eq, { duration: 2 }))
    s.wait(1)
})
```

### fadeIn and fadeOut

Fades can also travel with `shift` and change size with `scale`. With `lag`, a group fades in child by child.

```film paired label="A word rises into place, holds, and sinks away"
import { fadeIn, fadeOut, film, text } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const word = text('arrive', { font: 'text-serif', size: 280 })
    s.play(fadeIn(word, { shift: [0, 90], lag: 0.1, duration: 1.2 }))
    s.wait(0.6)
    s.play(fadeOut(word, { shift: [0, -90] }))
})
```

### grow

`grow` scales up from nothing. Pass `from` to grow out of a point, such as the tail of an arrow.

```film paired label="An arrow grows out of its tail point"
import { arrow, dot, film, grow } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    s.add(dot(22, 'ink').at(-600, 200))
    const pointer = arrow([-600, 200], [600, -200], { stroke: 'teal', width: 18, tip: 80 })
    s.play(grow(pointer, { from: [-600, 200], duration: 1.2 }))
    s.wait(1)
})
```

### erase

`erase` is the reverse of `draw`.

```film paired label="A wave draws and then erases along its length"
import { draw, erase, film, parametric } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const wave = parametric((u) => [-800 + 1600 * u, Math.sin(u * 14) * 220], 0, 1, { stroke: 'pink', width: 10 })
    s.play(draw(wave))
    s.wait(0.4)
    s.play(erase(wave))
})
```

`appear` and `vanish` show or hide a node with no transition.

## Change

### to

`to` animates any change. Make the change inside the callback, and the engine interpolates from the old state to the new one.

```film paired label="A dot moves, changes color, and grows in one motion"
import { dot, film, to } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const d = s.add(dot(70, 'blue').at(-550, 150))
    s.play(to(d, (n) => n.at(550, -150).color('yellow').scale(2.4), { duration: 1.5 }))
    s.wait(0.8)
})
```

### moveTo, shift, scaleBy, rotate, recolor, fade

These are short forms of `to` for one kind of change.

```film paired label="A square moves, turns, grows, and changes color in order"
import { film, moveTo, recolor, rect, rotate, scaleBy, seq } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const box = s.add(rect(240, 240, { fill: 'teal', stroke: null, radius: 12 }).at(-600, 0))
    s.play(seq(
        moveTo(box, [0, 0]),
        rotate(box, Math.PI / 2),
        scaleBy(box, 1.8),
        recolor(box, 'orange'),
    ))
    s.wait(0.6)
})
```

### along

`along` follows a path or the shape of another node. Set `orient` to turn the node along the way.

```film paired label="A triangle follows a figure-eight path and turns with it"
import { along, film, parametric, regularPolygon } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const road = s.add(parametric((t) => [Math.sin(t) * 700, Math.sin(t * 2) * 320], 0, Math.PI * 2, { stroke: 'grid', width: 6 }))
    const rider = s.add(regularPolygon(3, 48, { fill: 'yellow', stroke: null }).rotate(Math.PI / 2))
    s.play(along(rider, road, { orient: true, duration: 4 }))
})
```

### morph

`morph` turns one shape into another. Afterwards the target is on stage and the source is hidden, so later code always refers to the node you can see.

```film paired label="A square morphs into a circle and then into a letter"
import { circle, film, morph, rect, text } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const a = s.add(rect(520, 520, { fill: 'blue', stroke: null }))
    const b = circle(290, { fill: 'teal', stroke: null })
    const c = text('v', { font: 'text-serif', size: 900, color: 'yellow' })
    s.play(morph(a, b))
    s.wait(0.3)
    s.play(morph(b, c))
    s.wait(0.6)
})
```

### morphMatching

`morphMatching` morphs equations and labels by meaning. Glyphs on both sides travel to their new places, and the rest fade where they stand.

```film paired label="An equation rearranges as its terms travel"
import { film, morphMatching, tex, write } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const a = s.add(tex('a^2 + b^2 = c^2', { size: 150 }))
    s.play(write(a))
    const b = tex('a^2 = c^2 - b^2', { size: 150 })
    s.play(morphMatching(a, b, { duration: 1.6 }))
    s.wait(0.8)
})
```

### warp and applyMatrix

`warp` deforms shapes through any function of stage position. `applyMatrix` is the linear case.

```film paired label="A square grid shears under a matrix"
import { applyMatrix, film, plane } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const grid = s.add(plane({ unit: 200 }))
    s.wait(0.3)
    s.play(applyMatrix(grid, [[1, 1], [0, 1]], { duration: 2 }))
    s.wait(0.8)
})
```

```film paired label="A square grid bends under a smooth function of position"
import { film, plane, warp } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const grid = s.add(plane({ unit: 180 }))
    s.play(warp(grid, (x, y) => [x + Math.sin(y / 170) * 120, y + Math.sin(x / 170) * 120], { duration: 2.4 }))
    s.wait(0.8)
})
```

## Emphasis

These leave a node as they found it.

### indicate

```film paired label="One term of an equation swells and turns yellow, then returns"
import { film, indicate, tex } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const eq = s.add(tex('E = m c^2', { size: 190 }))
    s.wait(0.3)
    s.play(indicate(eq.part('c^2'), { scale: 1.3 }))
    s.wait(0.6)
})
```

### shake

```film paired label="A warning word shakes"
import { film, shake, text } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const word = s.add(text('careful', { font: 'text-serif', size: 300, color: 'red' }))
    s.wait(0.3)
    s.play(shake(word, { angle: 0.12 }))
    s.wait(0.6)
})
```

### circumscribe

```film paired label="A lit line traces around a word and runs off"
import { circumscribe, film, text } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const word = s.add(text('this one', { font: 'text-serif', size: 260 }))
    s.wait(0.2)
    s.play(circumscribe(word, { pad: 40, width: 7 }))
    s.wait(0.4)
})
```

### flash and ripple

```film paired label="A burst of rays and an expanding ring at a point"
import { dot, film, flash, ripple } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    s.add(dot(30, 'yellow'))
    s.play(flash([0, 0], { radius: 320, rays: 14 }))
    s.play(ripple([0, 0], { radius: 460, width: 8 }))
    s.wait(0.3)
})
```

### pulse

`pulse` sends a short lit segment along a line: a packet on an edge, or a signal on a wire.

```film paired label="A lit pulse travels down a curved line"
import { film, parametric, pulse } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const wire = s.add(parametric((u) => [-800 + 1600 * u, Math.sin(u * 7) * 200], 0, 1, { stroke: 'grid', width: 10 }))
    s.play(pulse(wire, { width: 16, glow: 20, duration: 1.6 }))
    s.wait(0.2)
})
```

## Composition

### par, seq, and lagged

`par` runs animations together. `seq` runs them in order. `lagged` starts each one after a fraction of the previous one has played.

```film paired label="A row of dots fades in as a wave from left to right"
import { dot, fadeIn, film, lagged } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const dots = Array.from({ length: 13 }, (_, i) => dot(30, 'teal').at(-720 + i * 120, Math.sin(i * 0.8) * 180))
    s.play(lagged(dots.map((d) => fadeIn(d, { scale: 0.1 })), { lag: 0.25 }), { duration: 2 })
    s.wait(0.8)
})
```

### delay, retime, and call

`delay` waits before an animation begins. `retime` changes the length or ease of an animation without changing what it does. `call` runs a function at a moment on the timeline.

`delay` gives a clean change from one sentence to the next. The old text fades before the new text can be read, so the two never overlap. Inside a `s.play` that has a `duration`, `seq(fadeOut(oldText), fadeIn(newText))` does the same.

```ts
import { delay, fadeIn, fadeOut, film, text } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film((s) => {
    const oldText = s.add(text('The old sentence', { size: 72 }))
    s.wait(1)
    const newText = text('The new sentence', { size: 72 })
    s.play(fadeOut(oldText, { duration: 0.15 }), delay(fadeIn(newText, { duration: 0.25 }), 0.1))
    s.wait(1)
})
```

### Value.to

Animate a number. Anything that reads it follows.

```film paired label="A readout counts from zero to one hundred"
import { decimal, film } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const n = s.value(0)
    s.add(decimal(() => n.value, { digits: 1, size: 220, color: 'yellow' }))
    s.play(n.to(100, { duration: 2.4 }))
    s.wait(0.6)
})
```

## Easing

Pass an `ease` to any animation. Names such as `smooth`, `smoother`, `easeOutCubic`, `rushInto`, `rushFrom`, and `bounce` are functions you import, and `overshoot()`, `spring()`, `wiggle()`, `cubicBezier()`, and `during()` build new ones.

```film paired label="Three dots travel with different easing"
import { bounce, dot, film, linear, moveTo, spring } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const row = (y: number, color: string) => s.add(dot(40, color).at(-650, y))
    const a = row(-220, 'blue'), b = row(0, 'yellow'), c = row(220, 'pink')
    s.play(
        moveTo(a, [650, -220], { ease: linear }),
        moveTo(b, [650, 0], { ease: spring() }),
        moveTo(c, [650, 220], { ease: bounce }),
        { duration: 2 },
    )
    s.wait(0.6)
})
```

# Guide: Camera

## Move and zoom

`s.camera` is a node. Its position is the point at the center of the frame. Its `sx` property is the zoom.

```film paired label="The camera zooms into one dot, then pulls back"
import { dot, film, Node, seq, to } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    for (let i = 0; i < 40; i++) {
        s.add(dot(14, i % 7 ? 'dim' : 'yellow').at(-760 + (i % 8) * 216, -360 + Math.floor(i / 8) * 180))
    }
    const look = (x: number, y: number, zoom: number) =>
        to(s.camera, (c: Node) => c.at(x, y).set('sx', zoom), { duration: 1.4 })
    s.play(seq(look(-112, -180, 4), look(0, 0, 1)))
})
```

## Keep titles in place

A pinned node ignores the camera. Use `.pin()` for titles, captions, and readouts that stay on the screen.

```film paired label="A grid slides under a pinned title"
import { film, Node, plane, text, to } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    s.add(plane({ unit: 160 }))
    s.add(text('This title is pinned.', { font: 'text-serif', size: 120 }).at(0, -380).pin())
    s.play(to(s.camera, (c: Node) => c.at(700, 300).set('sx', 1.6), { duration: 2 }))
    s.wait(0.5)
})
```

## Turn the view

Set `rotation` on the camera to turn the view.

```film paired label="The view rotates a quarter turn around the center"
import { film, Node, plane, to } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    s.add(plane({ unit: 200 }))
    s.play(to(s.camera, (c: Node) => c.set('rotation', Math.PI / 2), { duration: 2 }))
    s.wait(0.5)
})
```

Stroke widths scale with the zoom, as if the camera moved closer. For a line that keeps its screen width at every zoom, use a pinned node or set the width from the zoom in a `dynamic` drawing.

# Guide: CLI

## Films

### vizmatic new

Create a film from a starter that renders as written and passes the check.

```bash
npx vizmatic new intro --template explainer
```

The templates are `explainer`, `equation`, `architecture`, `chart`, and `deck`.

### vizmatic preview

Open a live preview with a timeline. The page reloads when you save.

```bash
npx vizmatic preview intro.ts --open
```

### vizmatic check

Inspect a film without rendering video. The check samples the timeline and reports marks off the canvas, overlapping text, and lines that cross text. Each finding has a time and a position. Use `--json` to read the report in a script.

A film whose lines run past the frame on purpose, such as a warped grid, sets `bleed: true` in its options. The check then ignores lines and shapes past the edge, and it still reports text that runs off the canvas.

```bash
npx vizmatic check intro.ts --look midnight,paper --json
```

The check looks where the film comes to rest, so it misses a problem that lasts only while something moves. `--motion` also inspects every frame. It reports a problem that appears only in motion as a warning, because it cannot tell a collision from one picture that replaces another. It reports 0.2 seconds or more with nothing visible as `film.blank`. `--content-top <px>` sets the canvas y where the content starts, so that a heading that stays up does not count as content.

```bash
npx vizmatic check intro.ts --motion --content-top 200
```

### vizmatic film

Export a film. See [Exporting](exporting.md) for the options.

```bash
npx vizmatic film intro.ts --out dist/films --look midnight,paper --quality high
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out <dir>` | The output folder. |
| `--look a,b` | Render in these looks. |
| `--format mp4,webm,gif,png,svg` | The output formats. |
| `--quality draft\|standard\|high\|master` | Encoder quality and motion blur. |
| `--fps <n>` | Frame rate. |
| `--width <n>` | Output width in pixels. |
| `--motion-blur <n>` | Sub-frames per frame. |
| `--shutter <0-1>` | The fraction of a frame the shutter stays open. |
| `--range a:b` | Render part of the timeline. |
| `--frame t,t` | Write stills at these times. |
| `--every <seconds>` | Write stills at this interval, across the film or its `--range`. |
| `--sheet` | Join the stills into contact sheets, each tile with its time. With no times, a sheet shows 12 moments spread over the film. |
| `--columns <n>` | Tiles in a row of a contact sheet. |
| `--poster` | Also write a poster frame. |
| `--workers <n>` | Rasterizer threads. |
| `--audio <file>` | Add a sound track. |
| `--background <color\|none>` | Replace the background. |
| `--ffmpeg <path>` | Use this FFmpeg. |
| `--json` | Print a report as JSON. |

### vizmatic looks and vizmatic objects

List the looks and the object library. Use `--json` in scripts and agents.

```bash
npx vizmatic looks --json
npx vizmatic objects --json
```

## Figures

Render TSX figures to PNG and SVG.

```bash
npx vizmatic ./frame.tsx --out ./figures --theme dark,light --format both
npx vizmatic check ./frame.tsx --theme dark,light --json
npx vizmatic gif ./animated-frame.tsx --out ./figures --theme dark,light --fps 20
```

Run `npx vizmatic --help` to see every option.

# Guide: Core concepts

## The stage

The stage is a coordinate space. The origin is the center of the frame, and y points down. The default stage is 1920 by 1080 units. You always author in these units, and the export width only changes how many pixels each unit gets.

```film paired label="A dot moves to each corner of the stage in turn"
import { dot, film, moveTo, seq } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const d = s.add(dot(40, 'yellow'))
    const corner = (x: number, y: number) => moveTo(d, [x, y], { duration: 0.6 })
    s.play(seq(
        corner(800, -400), corner(800, 400),
        corner(-800, 400), corner(-800, -400),
        corner(0, 0),
    ))
})
```

The stage also gives you `s.left`, `s.right`, `s.top`, and `s.bottom`, which are the edges in stage units.

## Nodes

Everything visible is a `Node`. A node with a path draws that path. A node with children groups them. Setter methods chain, so setup reads as one line.

```ts
import { circle, group, text } from 'vizmatic/stage'

const ring = circle(120, { stroke: 'blue', width: 4 }).glow(8)
const label = text('radius', { size: 36, color: 'dim' }).nextTo(ring, 'down', 24)
export const figure = group(ring, label).at(-300, 0)
```

Text and equations are also nodes. Each glyph is a child, so you can animate one letter or one term of an equation.

## The timeline

`s.play(...)` does not wait. It records keys on the timeline and moves the cursor forward, and your function finishes almost at once. Animations passed to one `s.play` run together. Use `seq` and `lagged` to arrange them in time.

```film paired label="Three squares fade in one after another while a label writes"
import { fadeIn, film, lagged, rect, text, write } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const boxes = [-400, 0, 400].map((x) =>
        rect(260, 260, { fill: 'teal', stroke: null, radius: 16 }).at(x, -60))
    const label = text('one play, two animations', { size: 72 }).at(0, 240)

    s.play(lagged(boxes.map((box) => fadeIn(box, { shift: [0, 40] }))), write(label))
    s.wait(1)
})
```

Because the function finishes before the first frame, code after a `play` sees the end state. This is why `eq.nextTo(graph)` is correct even when `graph` is still animating on screen.

## Why frames are pure

When the function returns, the film is compiled. A frame is then only a function of time: `film.frame(t)`. Nothing replays and nothing accumulates.

This gives you some useful properties:

- Seeking is immediate in both directions. On the [home page](../index.html), your scroll bar sets the time.
- Export can run frames on many threads, in any order, and encode them in sequence.
- Output is deterministic. The same source gives the same frames.

## Values and dynamic drawings

A `Value` is a number on the timeline. A `dynamic` node rebuilds its drawing on every frame from whatever it reads. Together they let geometry follow a number, as a secant follows its increment.

```film paired label="A sine wave whose frequency rises as a readout counts up"
import { axes, decimal, dynamic, film, Node } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const k = s.value(1)
    const graph = s.add(axes({ x: [0, 6.3], y: [-1.5, 1.5], width: 1300, height: 560, labels: false }).at(0, 60))
    s.add(dynamic(() => new Node(graph.plotPath((x) => Math.sin(k.value * x)))
        .stroke('yellow', 6).at(graph.get('x'), graph.get('y'))))
    s.add(decimal(() => k.value, { prefix: 'k = ', size: 72 }).at(0, -380))

    s.play(k.to(5, { duration: 3 }))
    s.play(k.to(1, { duration: 2 }))
})
```

A drawing inside `dynamic` should read values and return nodes. It should not change anything else, because it can run for any time in any order.

## Updaters

`s.update(node, fn)` runs a function on each frame and can set properties on a node that is already on stage. Use it when one node should follow another, without rebuilding geometry.

```ts
import { dot, film, moveTo, text } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film((s) => {
    const a = s.add(dot(20, 'yellow').at(-500, 0))
    const label = s.add(text('here', { size: 48 }))
    s.update(label, (node) => node.nextTo(a, 'up', 24))
    s.play(moveTo(a, [500, 0], { duration: 2 }))
})
```

## Assets load themselves

Fonts and the TeX engine load the first time a film asks for them. The compiler catches the request, waits, and then runs your function again. This is why a build function should have no side effects other than authoring on the stage.

# Guide: Cookbook

## A point that follows a curve

Drive a `dynamic` drawing from a `Value`. The dot and its guides stay true to the curve at any time.

```film paired label="A dot travels along a curve with a readout"
import { axes, draw, dot, dynamic, film, line } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const graph = s.add(axes({ x: [0, 6.3], y: [-1.4, 1.4], width: 1400, height: 700, labels: false }))
    const curve = graph.plot(Math.sin, { stroke: 'blue', width: 7 })
    s.play(draw(graph.lines), draw(curve), { duration: 1 })
    const x = s.value(0)
    s.add(dynamic(() => {
        const p = graph.world(x.value, Math.sin(x.value))
        return [
            line(graph.world(x.value, 0), p, { stroke: 'dim', width: 3, dash: [10, 12] }),
            dot(20, 'yellow').glow(20).at(p),
        ]
    }))
    s.play(x.to(6.28, { duration: 3 }))
})
```

## Trace a moving point

`traced` keeps the path of any point over a span of time.

```film paired label="A spirograph traces itself"
import { dot, dynamic, film, traced, type Vec } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const t = s.value(0)
    const point = (): Vec => {
        const a = t.value
        return [Math.cos(a) * 300 + Math.cos(a * 5.1) * 150, Math.sin(a) * 300 + Math.sin(a * 5.1) * 150]
    }
    s.add(traced(point, 0, 5, { color: 'teal', width: 4 }))
    s.add(dynamic(() => dot(16, 'yellow').at(point())))
    s.play(t.to(Math.PI * 6, { duration: 5, ease: (u) => u }))
})
```

## A signal through a system

Lines, labels, and pulses make a small architecture film. Connect the boxes first, and then send packets along the edges.

```film paired label="A request pulses through three services"
import { arrow, draw, fadeIn, film, lagged, pulse, rect, seq, text, group } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const box = (label: string, x: number) => group(
        rect(380, 200, { stroke: 'blue', width: 4, radius: 12 }),
        text(label, { size: 64 }).at(0, 0),
    ).at(x, 0)
    const boxes = [box('edge', -620), box('api', 0), box('db', 620)]
    const links = [arrow([-420, 0], [-200, 0], { stroke: 'dim', width: 6 }), arrow([200, 0], [420, 0], { stroke: 'dim', width: 6 })]
    s.play(lagged(boxes.map((b) => fadeIn(b, { shift: [0, 24] }))), { duration: 1 })
    s.play(...links.map((link) => draw(link)))
    const shaft = (i: number) => links[i]!.children[0]!
    s.play(seq(pulse(shaft(0), { duration: 0.7 }), pulse(shaft(1), { duration: 0.7 })))
    s.play(seq(pulse(shaft(1), { duration: 0.7 }), pulse(shaft(0), { duration: 0.7 })))
})
```

## Reveal a chart

Bars and lines are nodes, so a chart can arrive in order and call out one value.

```film paired label="Bars grow and one is highlighted"
import { barChart, film, grow, indicate, lagged } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const chart = s.add(barChart([
        { label: 'Mon', value: 3 }, { label: 'Tue', value: 5 }, { label: 'Wed', value: 9 }, { label: 'Thu', value: 4 },
    ], { width: 1200, height: 720 }))
    s.play(lagged(chart.bars.map((bar) => grow(bar, { from: bar.bottom })), { lag: 0.25 }), { duration: 1.4 })
    s.play(indicate(chart.bars[2]!, { color: 'yellow', scale: 1.05 }))
    s.wait(0.5)
})
```

## Build a logo sting

A glyph outline is a path, so a mark can draw itself and settle.

```film paired label="The letter v draws itself and a dot lands beside it"
import { dot, draw, fadeIn, film, overshoot, text } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film({ fps: 30 }, (s) => {
    const mark = s.add(text('v', { font: 'text-serif', size: 620 }))
    s.play(draw(mark, { duration: 1.4 }))
    const point = s.add(dot(36, 'yellow').glow(24).at(190, -160))
    s.play(fadeIn(point, { scale: 0.05, ease: overshoot() }))
    s.wait(0.6)
})
```

## Time things to a voiceover

Put a label at a moment with `s.at`, so one section does not push others around.

```ts
import { fadeIn, film, text } from 'vizmatic/stage'

export default film((s) => {
    const cue = (time: number, words: string, y: number) => {
        s.at(time, () => {
            s.play(fadeIn(s.add(text(words, { size: 72 }).at(0, y))))
        })
    }
    cue(0.5, 'First sentence.', -100)
    cue(3.2, 'Second sentence.', 40)
    s.wait(6)
})
```

`--audio narration.wav` pads or trims the sound to the film's length, so a film that ends early cuts off the voice. Make the film at least as long as the narration.

# Guide: Diagrams and density

## Two engines, one package

Films use the stage engine, which is vector animation from TypeScript functions. Figures use the component library, which lays out TSX elements and renders PNG, SVG, and GIF.

Use a figure when the reader studies the picture. Use a film when the change over time is the point.

```bash
npx vizmatic ./architecture.tsx --out ./figures --theme dark,light --format both
```

The [component explorer](../components.html) shows every component with live controls, and the [diagram builder](../playground.html) arranges them on a canvas.

## Titles are optional

A scene takes a title and a subtitle, and both are optional. Leave them out when the surrounding page already names the figure, and add a title when the visual needs them.

## A rich node

Graph nodes can carry more than a title. A node can have key and value rows, metrics with small trend lines, tags, an owner, and a footer. A reader then gets the facts from the figure without a second document.

```tsx
import { getThemeColors, GraphDiagram, Scene, type GraphDiagramEdge, type GraphDiagramNode, type ThemeMode } from 'vizmatic'

const nodes: GraphDiagramNode[] = [
    {
        id: 'api', label: 'Checkout API', detail: 'Go, 3 regions', icon: 'server', tone: 'blue', status: 'ok',
        rows: [{ key: 'replicas', value: '48' }, { key: 'deploy', value: 'blue/green' }],
        metrics: [{ label: 'p95', value: '184 ms' }, { label: 'errors', value: '0.02%' }],
    },
    { id: 'db', label: 'Orders', detail: 'Postgres 16', icon: 'database', tone: 'green' },
]
const edges: GraphDiagramEdge[] = [{ from: 'api', to: 'db', label: 'SQL, 2.1k/s' }]

export const width = 960
export const height = 420

export function create(theme: ThemeMode = 'dark') {
    const c = getThemeColors(theme)
    return (
        <Scene c={c} title="Checkout">
            <GraphDiagram c={c} nodes={nodes} edges={edges} width={900} height={320} />
        </Scene>
    )
}
```

## Database schemas

`EntityRelationshipDiagram` draws entity tables with attribute types, primary and foreign keys, uniqueness, nullability, and crow-foot endpoints. Each endpoint states how many records of that entity can match one record at the opposite end: `one`, `zero-or-one`, `one-or-many`, or `zero-or-many`.

```tsx
import { EntityRelationshipDiagram, getThemeColors, type ThemeMode } from 'vizmatic'

export const width = 960
export const height = 420

export function create(theme: ThemeMode = 'dark') {
    return <EntityRelationshipDiagram c={getThemeColors(theme)} width={960} height={420}
        title="Customer orders"
        entities={[
            { id: 'customers', attributes: [
                { name: 'id', type: 'uuid', primaryKey: true },
                { name: 'email', type: 'text', unique: true },
            ] },
            { id: 'orders', attributes: [
                { name: 'id', type: 'uuid', primaryKey: true },
                { name: 'customer_id', type: 'uuid', foreignKey: true },
            ] },
        ]}
        relationships={[{
            id: 'customer-orders', label: 'places',
            from: { entity: 'customers', attribute: 'id', cardinality: 'one' },
            to: { entity: 'orders', attribute: 'customer_id', cardinality: 'zero-or-many' },
        }]} />
}
```

This relationship gives each order exactly one customer; a customer may have no orders or many orders. For guest orders, mark `customer_id` nullable and use `zero-or-one` at the customer endpoint. Mark each primary-key attribute for a composite key, and pass an ordered attribute array at each relationship endpoint to show a composite relationship. Set `identifying` when the parent key forms part of the child primary key; the relationship then uses a solid line.

The component checks duplicate names, endpoint references, composite arity, nullable primary keys, and canvas dimensions. Tables expand for long names instead of reducing text size. Exported SVGs retain an accessible schema summary, entity constraints, and relationship cardinalities. The [checkout example](../examples.html#example-entity-relationship) includes guest orders and a composite line-item key.

## Accessible chart exports

Charts keep their titles and data summaries in exported SVGs. Use `title` to name the chart and `description` to explain its takeaway or context. The generated summary also retains category values, series, coordinates, or intervals. A labeled sparkline can provide the same metadata; an unlabeled sparkline stays decorative beside its surrounding metric.

## Density

Every component reads its type, spacing, strokes, and corner radius from one set of tokens. One source can render as a dense engineering figure or as a slide.

| Density | Use |
|---|---|
| `dense` | The default. Small type at 10 to 12 px, hairlines, and tight gutters. |
| `compact` | A little more air, for docs and dashboards. |
| `comfortable` | The sizes the components were first designed at. |
| `presentation` | Large type and strokes, for a room. |
| a number | A direct scale. `0.9` is slightly dense, and `1.25` is large. |

Set it on a scene.

```tsx
import { CalloutCard, getThemeColors, Scene, type ThemeMode } from 'vizmatic'

export function create(theme: ThemeMode = 'dark') {
    const c = getThemeColors(theme)
    return (
        <Scene c={c} title="Same content, larger" density="presentation">
            <CalloutCard c={c} title="Density is one prop" detail="Nothing else in the source changes." />
        </Scene>
    )
}
```

Or set it for a whole render.

```ts
import { renderToPng } from 'vizmatic'
import type { ReactElement } from 'react'

export async function renderBoth(figure: ReactElement): Promise<void> {
    await renderToPng(figure, { width: 1400, height: 800, outputPath: 'figure.png', density: 'dense' })
    await renderToPng(figure, { width: 1400, height: 800, outputPath: 'slide.png', density: 'presentation' })
}
```

## Check before you publish

`vizmatic check` reports overflow, contrast, small text, overlapping labels, and connector congestion. It works in both themes and can write JSON.

```bash
npx vizmatic check ./architecture.tsx --theme dark,light --json
```

## Keep the source

A figure is a TSX file. Keep it beside the document it illustrates, review it in a pull request, and render it in CI. Dark and light come from the same file.

# Guide: Editable scenes

Use `vizmatic-scene` when an application stores editable TSX from a user or an
agent. The regular `vizmatic` CLI loads trusted Node modules; it is not the entry
point for running editable source inside an application.

```bash
vizmatic-scene --input examples/pressure-mechanism.scene.json --output pressure.mp4
```

The JSON request contains `source`, `width`, `height`, `duration`, optional `fps`
(24 by default), `theme`, `cues`, `seed`, and optional preview `time`. All times
are **seconds**. Output is PNG for an exact preview time or a silent H.264 MP4.
FFmpeg must be on PATH for MP4. Narration, captions and final assembly remain the
calling application's responsibility.

```typescript
import { renderSceneFrame, renderSceneVideo } from 'vizmatic'

const scene = {
    width: 1920, height: 1080, duration: 12, fps: 24, theme: 'dark' as const,
    cues: { reveal: 3.2 }, seed: 0,
    source: `const amount = ease(cue('reveal', 2));
<svg width={width} height={height}>
    <rect width={width} height={height} fill={c.bg}/>
    <circle cx={lerp(300, 1600, amount)} cy={540} r={70} fill={c.info}/>
    <text x={150} y={200} fontSize={64} fill={c.textPrimary}>Follow the mechanism</text>
</svg>`,
}
await renderSceneFrame({ ...scene, time: 4, outputPath: './preview.png' })
await renderSceneVideo({ ...scene, outputPath: './scene.mp4' })
```

For editor previews, add `outputScale: 0.5` to either renderer and
`previewFps: 12` to `renderSceneVideo`. The renderer still evaluates and lays out
the original logical `width`, `height`, `duration`, `fps`, `frame`, and cues; it
only rasterizes fewer pixels and samples fewer video frames. `outputScale` must
be from 0.25 to 1 and produce even integer dimensions. `previewFps` must be an
integer from 1 to the scene's logical fps. These options also work in the
`vizmatic-scene` JSON request (`previewFps` is MP4-only).

Preview metadata reports effective `width`, `height`, `fps`, and `frameCount`,
plus `logicalWidth`, `logicalHeight`, `logicalFps`, `logicalFrameCount`,
`outputScale`, and, for video, `previewFps`. Its input hash binds the effective
output settings. Omitting the options preserves full-quality rendering and its
existing input hash.

Source uses local JavaScript/TypeScript declarations and helper components followed
by one JSX root. Imports, exports and module wrappers are not supported. Vizmatic
JSX primitives are provided automatically. SVG geometry and `<text>`/`<tspan>` use
the bundled fonts through Resvg, including inside HTML layouts. `Scene`, `Board`,
`CanvasItem`, charts and other trusted Vizmatic components use the same rendering
path in previews and video frames. Function-valued props are unsupported; calculate
formatted values and geometry in the source before returning JSX.

| Source value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `width`, `height` | Logical canvas dimensions before optional preview scaling |
| `time` / `t`, `duration` | Current position and narration duration in seconds |
| `progress`, `frame`, `fps` | Normalized progress, zero-based frame and cadence |
| `theme`, `c` | Theme name and frozen Vizmatic theme colors |
| `cues` | Named narration cue positions in seconds |
| `seed`, `Math.random()` | Explicit uint32 seed and deterministic random sequence |
| `clamp(x, min=0, max=1)`, `lerp(a,b,p)` | Clamp and linear interpolation |
| `ease(p)`, `easeInOut(p)`, `easeOut(p)` | Clamped smoothstep and cubic ease-out |
| `cue(name, span=1)` | Progress from a named cue over a span in seconds |

A missing named cue fails preparation rather than inventing a timing. Applications
should resolve production cues against actual narration and label estimated preview
cues as estimates. Source can be evaluated without Node rendering through
`evaluateSceneSource` or `prepareScene` from `vizmatic/scene-runtime`, suitable for
a browser Worker. The same evaluator produces a validated JSON scene graph in both
environments.

### Realtime browser previews

Use `vizmatic/scene-browser` in a dedicated module Worker for local editing,
scrubbing and playback. It uses the same bounded QuickJS evaluator, fonts, trusted
components and Resvg rasterizer as the Node scene renderer. Both native SVG and
Vizmatic layouts are supported. Compile once per source revision and render each
new time locally; a full MP4 or HTTP request is not required for playback.

```typescript
// Inside a dedicated Worker. The application fetches these assets from its own origin.
import { createBrowserSceneRenderer } from 'vizmatic/scene-browser'

const renderer = await createBrowserSceneRenderer({
    quickjsWasm, resvgWasm,
    layoutWasm: () => loadLayoutWasm(),
    fonts: { interRegular, interSemiBold, interBold, jetBrainsMono, notoSans, notoSansMath },
    emoji: () => loadOfflineEmoji(), // Optional, loaded only for an emoji glyph.
})
const prepared = await renderer.prepare(scene, { outputScale: 0.5 })
const frame = await prepared.render(4)
postMessage(frame, [frame.pixels.buffer])
```

The three WASM inputs and six font inputs are `ArrayBuffer`s. `layoutWasm` also
accepts a loader, so native SVG previews never load Satori's chunk or layout WASM.
Their hashes are checked before initialization, and initialization is reused. The
optional emoji loader returns the parsed pinned emoji JSON; it is checked and
cached on first use. Satori's standalone build embeds its HarfBuzz runtime.

At application build time, `getSceneBrowserAssetPaths()` from
`vizmatic/browser-assets` resolves `quickjsWasm`, `layoutWasm`, `resvgWasm`,
`fonts`, and `emojiBrotli` to installed local files. Copy them to your static assets;
decompress the emoji Brotli file at build time if the browser does not support
Brotli streams. The browser entry is prebundled ESM and requires no Node shims or
special file loaders. Keep it out of the initial application bundle and load its
Worker when a preview becomes visible. Keep ESM code splitting enabled in your
application's Worker build to preserve the deferred Satori download.

Frames contain owned, transferable RGBA `pixels`, effective `width` and `height`,
`time`, source and input hashes, runtime version, and `timings` in milliseconds.
Draw them with `ImageData` on a canvas. A single unchanged graph retains one backing
raster while each caller receives an independent pixel buffer. Logical scene
dimensions, fps, cues and frame globals remain unchanged by `outputScale`.

Keep only the latest queued frame, stop playback when hidden, and terminate the
Worker on an application deadline or when its editor closes. QuickJS limits author
execution; the Worker deadline also bounds trusted layout and rasterization. Keep
narration alignment and final export validation in the application's server path.
`pnpm check:scene-browser` checks real Chromium Worker rendering against Node pixels,
isolation, error recovery and playback without network requests.

Editable JavaScript executes inside QuickJS WebAssembly with no host objects,
callbacks, filesystem, network, browser storage or module loader. Each frame gets
a fresh context, a 64 MiB guest memory limit, a 256 KiB stack and a 250 ms evaluation
deadline. Only bounded JSON reaches trusted components. External image references,
resource URLs, event handlers, raw HTML and executable props are rejected. The
renderer uses fingerprinted package fonts and emoji assets, with no environment
overrides, system fonts or network fallback. Local SVG fragment references work.

Limits are 128 KiB of source, 2 MiB of serialized graph, 2,000 JSX elements, 64
levels of nesting, at most 1,920 pixels per edge and 2,073,600 pixels per canvas,
120 seconds per scene, 1–60 fps and 3,600 frames. Nested SVGs also share a per-frame
allocation budget. Run the CLI in a subprocess with a bounded environment, captured
stderr, memory limit and total deadline; the QuickJS deadline governs author code,
while the caller's process deadline also covers trusted layout and FFmpeg.

The CLI writes one JSON metadata line on success. `runtimeVersion`,
`sourceSha256`, `inputSha256`, `assetSha256`, `fontAssetsSha256`, dimensions,
duration, fps, timeline `frameCount`, output byte count and output path identify the
result. `assetSha256` hashes the actual output file. Preview metadata adds `time`;
MP4 adds `encodedDuration`. Cache inputs include the runtime, exact source, cues,
seed, theme, dimensions, duration, cadence, pinned assets, output kind and preview
time. Like the existing video API, MP4 duration rounds to the nearest frame.
Existing output files survive a failed render.

# Guide: Embedding the player

## The element

`<vz-film>` plays a compiled film. Importing `vizmatic/stage/browser` registers the element. Bundle your film with it, and then add the element to your page.

```html
<script type="module" src="./stage.js"></script>
<vz-film src="./my-film.js" autoplay loop label="A curve becomes its tangent"></vz-film>
```

The element compiles the film when it scrolls within reach, pauses when it leaves the screen, and honors `prefers-reduced-motion` by showing the final frame.

Your film and the engine must share one module, because that module holds the timeline clock. A bundler with code splitting does this for you.

## Attributes

| Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `src` | The URL of a module whose default export is a film. |
| `autoplay` | Play when visible. |
| `loop` | Start again at the end. |
| `stepped` | Stop at each chapter. See [Presentations](presentations.md). |
| `nocontrols` | Hide the controls. |
| `start` | Start at this time in seconds. |
| `look` | Compile in this look, such as `paper`. |
| `background` | Replace the look's background, so the film sits directly on your page. |
| `label` | The text alternative for assistive technology. Always set this. |

## Events

| Event | Detail |
|---|---|
| `ready` | `{ film, player }`, once the film is compiled. |
| `timeupdate` | `{ time }`, on every painted frame. |
| `error` | `{ error }`, if the film fails to load. The element also shows the message. |

## Drive it from your page

`element.controller` is a `FilmPlayer`. Its `seek` method is cheap enough to call on every scroll event. This is how the home page works.

```ts
export function scrubWithScroll(section: HTMLElement, element: HTMLElement & { controller: { seek(time: number): void; film: { duration: number } } | null }): void {
    window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
        const box = section.getBoundingClientRect()
        const amount = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, -box.top / (box.height - innerHeight)))
        const player = element.controller
        if (player) player.seek(amount * player.film.duration)
    }, { passive: true })
}
```

## Without the element

Use `FilmPlayer` on your own canvas when you want your own controls.

```ts
import { compileFilm, FilmPlayer, film, text, write } from 'vizmatic/stage/browser'

const intro = film((s) => {
    s.play(write(s.add(text('Hello', { font: 'text-serif', size: 200 }))))
})

export async function mount(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement): Promise<FilmPlayer> {
    return new FilmPlayer(canvas, await compileFilm(intro), { autoplay: true, loop: true })
}
```

## Take input

Because a frame is computed when it is needed, a film can read from your page. Put your state in plain variables, read them in a `dynamic` node, and call `player.seek(player.time)` when they change. The [matrix laboratory](../index.html#lab) on the home page works this way.

## Fonts

In the browser, the engine fetches TrueType fonts from an `assets/fonts` folder beside its module. Call `setAssetBase(url)` if they live elsewhere.

# Guide: Exporting

## From the command line

```bash
npx vizmatic film my-film.ts --out ./out
npx vizmatic film my-film.ts --format mp4,webm,gif --quality high
npx vizmatic film my-film.ts --look midnight,paper --width 3840
```

MP4 export needs FFmpeg with `libx264`. WebM also needs `libvpx-vp9`. The CLI writes a manifest with sizes and timings beside the files.

## Quality

| Quality | Use | H.264 CRF | Motion blur |
|---|---|---|---|
| `draft` | Checking timing. | 26 | off |
| `standard` | The default. | 18 | off |
| `high` | Publishing. | 15 | 4 samples |
| `master` | Archiving and re-encoding. | 11 | 8 samples |

Motion blur evaluates every sampled time and averages real sub-frames across the shutter. `--motion-blur` and `--shutter` set these directly.

MP4 files stay at H.264 level 4.2 at 1080p60, so they play in QuickTime, Quick Look, and on Apple devices. To join another clip to a film without encoding it again, encode the clip with `filmEncoderSettings(quality)` from `vizmatic/stage/export`. QuickTime reads one set of decoder settings from the start of a file, and it stops at a clip that uses different ones.

## Resolution

A film is authored in stage units, so `--width` changes only the pixel count. MP4 and WebM need even dimensions, so the export rounds an odd width or height up to the next even number.

## Stills

`--frame` writes PNG files at the given times. `--poster` also writes the fullest moment at rest, or the time you set with `film({ poster: 12 })`.

```bash
npx vizmatic film my-film.ts --frame 2.5,7 --width 1280
```

`--every` samples the film at an interval, in place of a list of times. `--sheet` joins the stills into one PNG, a contact sheet, with the time under each tile. With `--sheet`, `--width` is the width of one tile and defaults to 480. A sheet has up to 6 rows, and a longer list of times continues on the next sheet.

```bash
npx vizmatic film my-film.ts --every 5 --sheet --columns 4
npx vizmatic film my-film.ts --range 30:60 --every 1 --sheet
```

In code, `renderFilmSheet(film, times, path, { width, columns })` from `vizmatic/stage/export` writes one sheet.

## SVG

A frame is a list of vector paths, so it exports as standalone SVG with no fonts needed.

```bash
npx vizmatic film my-film.ts --format svg --frame 7
```

## Part of a film

`--range` renders part of the timeline, which helps while you adjust one section.

```bash
npx vizmatic film my-film.ts --range 12:18 --quality draft
```

## Sound

`--audio` adds a track. The audio is padded or trimmed to the film's length. FFmpeg must include AAC.

```bash
npx vizmatic film my-film.ts --audio narration.wav
```

Captions from `s.caption` export as a WebVTT file beside the video.

## From code

```ts
import { compileFilm, film, text, write } from 'vizmatic/stage'
import { renderFilmFrame, renderFilmVideo } from 'vizmatic/stage/export'

const intro = film((s) => {
    s.play(write(s.add(text('Hello', { font: 'text-serif', size: 200 }))))
})

export async function render(): Promise<void> {
    const compiled = await compileFilm(intro, { look: 'paper' })
    await renderFilmVideo(compiled, 'out/intro.mp4', { quality: 'high' })
    await renderFilmFrame(compiled, compiled.duration, 'out/intro.png', { width: 1280 })
}
```

## Bloom

Bloom is part of a look, and export applies it after rasterizing. Pass `bloom` on the film to change it. Set it to `0` for line art that needs exact colors.

## Speed

Each frame compiles to SVG on the main thread and rasterizes on a worker. The exporter chooses the thread count from your CPU count and frame size. Use `--workers` to change it. See the [benchmarks](../benchmarks.html) for measured numbers from the component renderer.

Each worker can reuse its last completed RGBA result when every SVG sample, dimension, bloom setting, and background value is identical. This applies to generated frames with prepared, embedded image assets. Raw SVG jobs and unresolved image references always rasterize again. Updaters and every shutter sample still run before this comparison.

The worker retains one private result, capped at 64 MiB of pixels and an 8 MiB serialized-key allowance. Returned buffers are separate copies. Render planning includes this retained memory when choosing workers.

# Guide: Figure recipes

## Full frame example

Create `frames/agent-pipeline.tsx`:

```jsx
width = 1040;
height = 560;

<Scene
  title="Agent visual pipeline"
  subtitle="prompt -> TSX scene -> render -> files"
  gap={26}
>
  <Flow
    connectorTone="purple"
    stages={[
      {
        eyebrow: "input",
        title: "Prompt",
        subtitle: "intent and constraints",
        tone: "blue",
        lines: ["domain language", "audience", "theme tokens"],
        width: 190,
      },
      {
        eyebrow: "contract",
        title: "Scene spec",
        subtitle: "typed structure",
        tone: "purple",
        lines: ["cards", "flows", "charts", "tables"],
        width: 190,
      },
      {
        eyebrow: "render",
        title: "Node renderer",
        subtitle: "headless output",
        tone: "cyan",
        lines: ["layout", "theme", "checks"],
        width: 190,
      },
      {
        eyebrow: "output",
        title: "PNG / SVG / GIF",
        subtitle: "rendered files",
        tone: "green",
        lines: ["dark + light", "alpha", "manifest"],
        width: 190,
      },
    ]}
  />
  <Row width="100%" gap={14}>
    <CalloutCard
      title="Use scene primitives"
      detail="Common diagrams do not need hand-written SVG paths or x/y coordinates."
      tone="purple"
      width={470}
    />
    <CalloutCard
      title="Use theme tokens"
      detail="Tokens set color, typography, radius, spacing, and contrast."
      tone="green"
      width={470}
    />
  </Row>
</Scene>
```

Render it:

```bash
vizmatic frames --out public/vizmatic --theme dark,light --watermark "Your Product" --watermark-image ./logo.svg --watermark-position top-right
```

Generated `manifest.json` includes each output file plus its theme, path, width, and height.

The static CLI defaults to PNG. Add `--format svg` for vector output or `--format both` to render PNG and SVG together in every requested theme.

PNG and SVG renders have transparent backgrounds by default. Use the theme background when the image needs an opaque canvas:

```bash
vizmatic frames --out public/vizmatic --theme dark,light --background theme
```

Or set it in the frame:

```jsx
<Scene background={c.bg} title="Opaque article figure">
  <Flow stages={[{ title: "Theme fill", tone: "purple" }]} />
</Scene>
```

CSS alpha colors are preserved in PNG/SVG backgrounds. Use `<Scene background="rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.5)">` or `--background 'rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.5)'` for a semi-transparent canvas. Leave the background unset for fully transparent output. Contrast checks composite alpha text and nested backgrounds over known solid surfaces; a transparent canvas has no known host-page backdrop.

When a CLI frame omits `width` or `height`, Vizmatic starts at `960x540` and grows that axis if content overflows. Set `autoSize = false` when dimensions must remain fixed and clipping should fail the render.

Bare CLI frames do not need imports, `defineIllustration`, or `c` props. Use `c` for explicit tokens such as `background={c.bg}`. `Scene` title and subtitle are optional. Use a full module for other dependencies, reusable helpers, animation exports, or direct renderer APIs.

Frame modules can export a watermark element instead of using CLI flags:

```jsx
import { Watermark } from "vizmatic"

export const watermark = (
  <Watermark position="bottom-right" opacity={0.82}>
    <div style={{
      display: "flex",
      alignItems: "center",
      gap: 6,
      color: "#7c3aed",
      fontFamily: "Inter",
      fontWeight: 800,
      fontSize: 12,
    }}>
      <img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,..." width={14} height={14} />
      Your Product
    </div>
  </Watermark>
)
```

Render a sampled state timeline with `createAnimation(theme)`:

```bash
vizmatic gif frames/animated-pipeline.tsx --out public/vizmatic --theme dark,light --fps 20 --watermark "Your Product" --watermark-image ./logo.svg --watermark-position top-right --scale 1
```

## Animated frames

An animated module exports `createAnimation(theme)` for GIF or MP4 output and keeps `create(theme)` for a static or reduced-motion fallback. Define state once, then describe holds, eased transitions, instant keyframes, and parallel property tracks. Vizmatic samples absolute timeline time and renders every frame.

For MP4, export `createAnimation(theme)` and run `vizmatic video frames/lesson.tsx --out public/videos --theme dark --fps 30`. This requires Node.js 20 or newer and FFmpeg with the `libx264` encoder; add `--audio narration.wav` for AAC audio. The CLI pads or trims audio to the animation duration. Exported canvas dimensions after `--scale` must be positive even integers. MP4 uses an opaque theme background by default and supports 1–120 fps independently of GIF cadence. The browser builder exports GIF; MP4 runs in Node.js. Keep `.vtt` or `.srt` captions as separate files and synchronize them to the finished timeline. Use `examples/videos/request-lifecycle.tsx` as a short, generic starting point and `examples/videos/signal-to-story.tsx` for a longer film with parallel tracks, path tracing, camera motion, and an ending held on screen. Animate the data or mechanism the lesson explains; avoid decorative logo or icon reveals. For package consumers, install Vizmatic and React in the project and FFmpeg separately. In the repository, `pnpm render:video` regenerates the showcase media.

```jsx
import React from "react"
import { Scene, defineAnimation, getThemeColors, hold, keyframe, tween, type ThemeMode } from "vizmatic"

export const width = 1040
export const height = 560

type State = { operation: number; progress: number }

function buildFrame(theme: ThemeMode, state: State) {
  const c = getThemeColors(theme)
  return (
    <Scene c={c} title={state.operation === 0 ? "Broadcast" : "AllReduce"}>
      <div style={{ display: "flex", width: "100%", height: 260, position: "relative" }}>
        <div style={{
          display: "flex",
          position: "absolute",
          left: 40 + state.progress * 720,
          top: 90,
          padding: "10px 16px",
          borderRadius: 8,
          background: c.accent,
          color: c.textOnColor,
        }}>chunk</div>
      </div>
    </Scene>
  )
}

export function createAnimation(theme: ThemeMode) {
  return defineAnimation<State>({
    initial: { operation: 0, progress: 0 },
    timeline: [
      hold(500, "Broadcast input"),
      tween({ progress: 1 }, { duration: 900, easing: "ease-in-out", label: "Broadcast" }),
      hold(500, "Broadcast output"),
      keyframe({ operation: 1, progress: 0 }),
      tween({ progress: 1 }, { duration: 900, easing: "ease-in-out", label: "AllReduce" }),
    ],
    fps: 20,
    render: (state) => buildFrame(theme, state),
  })
}

export function create(theme: ThemeMode = "dark") {
  return buildFrame(theme, { operation: 1, progress: 1 })
}

export default create("dark")
```

Top-level timeline steps run sequentially. Properties inside one `tween` move together. Use `parallel({ x: [...], opacity: [...] })` when property tracks need different delays or durations. Default interpolation supports finite numbers; use a custom `interpolate(from, to, progress)` for colors, points, or other values. Infinite loops should finish on the same visual state where they start. Fade moving content out and reset it with a zero-duration `keyframe` while hidden instead of reversing a one-way operation. `createScenes(theme)` remains supported for deliberate scene cuts and pixel `fade`/`appear` transitions.

## Choose primitives

Use Vizmatic primitives for common layouts. Use raw SVG only for geometry the component set cannot express.

Shared values:

- `ThemeMode`: `"dark" | "light"`.
- `ToneName`: `"blue" | "purple" | "green" | "warm" | "cyan" | "pink" | "red" | "critical" | "neutral" | "sunset" | "ocean" | "dark"`.
- `ColorName`: `"primary" | "secondary" | "positive" | "warning" | "critical" | "info" | "accent" | "neutral"`.
- `FlexAlign`: `"start" | "center" | "end" | "stretch"`.
- `FlexJustify`: `"start" | "center" | "end" | "space-between" | "space-around"`.
- Bare CLI frames omit `c` props. The local `c` object remains available for explicit values such as `background={c.bg}`.
- Full modules pass the `c: ThemeColors` value from `defineIllustration((c) => ...)` to visual components.
- PNG/SVG renders are alpha-transparent by default. Use `--background theme`, `background: "theme"`, or `<Scene background={c.bg}>` for opaque theme fill.
- Omitted CLI dimensions auto-grow on overflow. Explicit `width` / `height` remain fixed and fail on clipping.

## Component API

Frame helpers:

- `defineIllustration(build, defaultTheme?)`: `build: (c: ThemeColors) => ReactElement`, `defaultTheme?: ThemeMode = "dark"`. Returns `{ create(theme), default }`.
- `Canvas`: `children?`, `c`, `padding?: number = 40`, `justify?: "center" | "flex-start" | "space-between" | "space-around" = "center"`, `background?: string`. Default root background is alpha-transparent during PNG/SVG rendering.
- `Board`: `children?`, `c`, `width?: number = 960`, `height?: number = 540`, `background?: string`. Fixed relative canvas with a transparent default background; clips content outside its bounds. Match frame dimensions to the board. Dimensions must be finite, greater than zero, and at most 8192.
- `CanvasItem`: `children?`, `x: number`, `y: number`, `width?: number`, `height?: number`. Absolute position in logical board pixels. Coordinates must be finite. Explicit dimensions must be greater than zero and at most 8192; they supply the child's width/height props. With both dimensions set, chart primitives scale proportionally to fit their complete plotting layer, headings, legends, and footer inside the item. Use literal coordinates and dimensions for preview move/resize controls.
- `Scene`: `c`, `children`, `title?`, `subtitle?`, `padding?: number = 40`, `gap?: number = 24`, `justify?: "center" | "flex-start" | "space-between" | "space-around" = "flex-start"`, `align?: FlexAlign = "stretch"`, `contentWidth?: number | string = "100%"`, `background?`, `contentStyle?: React.CSSProperties`. Title/subtitle are optional and the title bar is omitted when no title is provided. Use `background={c.bg}` for an opaque theme frame.
- `TitleBar`: `title`, `subtitle?`, `c`.

Layout primitives:

- `Row` / `Column`: `children`, `gap?: number = 12`, `align?: FlexAlign = "center"`, `justify?: FlexJustify = "center"`, `wrap?: boolean = false`, `width?: number | string`, `height?: number | string`, `style?: React.CSSProperties`.
- `Stack`: `children`, `direction?: "vertical" | "horizontal" = "vertical"`, `gap?: number = 12`, `align?: "start" | "center" | "end" | "stretch" = "center"`, `wrap?: boolean = false`.
- `Panel`: `title`, `c`, `children?`, `subtitle?`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `footer?`, `width?`, `minWidth?`, `height?`, `minHeight?`, `padding?: number | string = 14`, `radius?: number = 8`, `gap?: number = 10`, `align?: FlexAlign = "stretch"`, `justify?: FlexJustify = "start"`, `shadow?: boolean = true`, `background?`, `borderColor?`, `titleFontSize?`, `accentWidth?: number = 34`, `accentHeight?: number = 4`, `bodyStyle?: React.CSSProperties`.
- `Card`: `children?`, `c`, `title?`, `subtitle?`, `tone?`, `footer?`, `width?`, `minWidth?`, `height?`, `minHeight?`, `padding?: number | string = 20`, `radius?: number = 8`, `gap?`, `align?: FlexAlign = "stretch"`, `justify?: FlexJustify = "start"`, `shadow?: boolean = false`, `background?`, `borderColor?`, `bodyStyle?: React.CSSProperties`.
- `WindowFrame`: `c`, `children?`, `title?`, `variant?: "window" | "browser" | "terminal" = "window"`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `dots?: boolean = true`, `width?`, `minWidth?`, `height?`, `minHeight?`, `padding?: number | string = 16`, `radius?: number = 10`, `shadow?: boolean = true`, `background?`, `bodyStyle?: React.CSSProperties`.

Cards, labels, and compact UI:

- `TextLabel`: `text`, `c`, `variant?: keyof typography = "body"`, `color?`, `fontSize?`, `fontWeight?`, `width?`, `align?: "left" | "center" | "right" = "left"`, `math?: boolean = false`, `mono?: boolean = false`.
- `MathText`: `text`. Returns formatted unicode-ish math text for simple `_` and `^` notation.
- `formatMathText(text)`: `text: string`.
- `Icon`: `name`, `c`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `color?`, `size?: number = 24`, `strokeWidth?: number = 2`, `label?`, `muted?: boolean = false`. `IconName` includes presentation icons plus architecture icons: `browser`, `bucket`, `cache`, `cloud`, `cluster`, `container`, `database`, `firewall`, `gateway`, `load-balancer`, `mobile`, `monitor`, `network`, `queue`, `server`, `storage`, `stream`, and `user`.
- `ToneStrip`: `tone`, `width?: number = 34`, `height?: number = 4`.
- `StepCard`: `title`, `c`, `subtitle?`, `eyebrow?`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `width?: number | string = 210`, `minWidth?`, `minHeight?: number | string = 74`, `padding?: number | string = "12px 14px"`, `radius?: number = 8`, `shadow?: boolean = true`, `align?: "left" | "center" = "center"`, `math?: boolean = false`.
- `MetricCard`: `label`, `value`, `c`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `detail?`, `width?`, `minWidth?`, `minHeight?: number | string = 74`, `padding?: number | string = "10px 12px"`, `radius?: number = 8`, `shadow?: boolean = true`, `align?: "left" | "center" = "center"`, `math?: boolean = false`, `valueMono?: boolean = true`, `valueFontSize?: number = 22`, `valueColor?`.
- `CalloutCard`: `c`, `children?`, `title?`, `detail?`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `width?`, `minHeight?`, `padding?: number | string = 12`, `titleFontSize?: number`, `detailFontSize?: number`, `filled?: boolean = true`, `align?: "left" | "center" = "center"`.
- `ValuePill`: `label`, `value`, `c`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `detail?`, `width?: number | string = 112`, `math?: boolean = false`.
- `BadgePill`: `text`, `c`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `width?`, `minWidth?: number | string = 34`, `height?: number | string = 20`, `padding?: number | string = "0 8px"`, `radius?: number = 6`, `fontSize?: number = 11`, `mono?: boolean = true`, `filled?: boolean = false`, `math?: boolean = false`.
- `Badge`: `label`, `c`, `color?: ColorName = "primary"`.
- `GradientChip`: `title`, `c`, `subtitle?`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `gradient?`, `width?`, `minWidth?`, `height?`, `minHeight?: number | string = 78`, `padding?: number | string = "0 18px"`, `radius?: number = 8`, `shadow?: boolean = true`, `align?: "left" | "center" = "left"`, `subtitleMono?: boolean = true`, `math?: boolean = false`.
- `EquationCard`: `title`, `formula`, `c`, `tone?: ToneName = "purple"`, `result?`, `detail?`, `width?: number | string = 190`, `height?`, `math?: boolean = false`, `align?: "left" | "center" = "left"`.
- `DetailList`: `items`, `c`, `tone?`, `gap?: number = 7`, `padding?: number | string = "7px 8px"`, `fontSize?: number = 11`, `mono?: boolean = false`, `math?: boolean = false`.

Lists, tables, status, and comparison:

- `ProgressRow`: `label`, `value: number`, `valueLabel?`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `muted?: boolean = false`, `c`, `labelWidth?: number = 42`, `valueWidth?: number = 38`, `barHeight?: number = 8`, `fontSize?: number = 11`. Keep `value` in `[0, 1]`.
- `ProgressList`: `rows: ProgressRowSpec[]`, `c`, `gap?: number = 8`, `labelWidth?`, `valueWidth?`, `barHeight?`, `fontSize?`. `ProgressRowSpec`: `label`, `value`, `valueLabel?`, `tone?`, `muted?`.
- `StatusRow`: `label`, `detail?`, `status?: "check" | "cross" | "warn" | "info" | "pending" | "dot" = "check"`, `tone?`, `c`, `boxed?: boolean = true`, `fontSize?: number = 11`, `width?`, `math?: boolean = false`.
- `StatusList`: `rows: StatusRowSpec[]`, `c`, `gap?: number = 7`, `boxed?: boolean = true`, `fontSize?`, `width?`, `math?: boolean = false`. `StatusRowSpec`: `label`, `detail?`, `status?`, `tone?`.
- `Timeline`: `events: TimelineEventSpec[]`, `c`, `title?`, `subtitle?`, `direction?: "vertical" | "horizontal" = "vertical"`, `width?`, `eventWidth?`, `gap?: number = 12`, `markerSize?: number = 14`, `math?: boolean = false`. `TimelineEventSpec`: `title`, `detail?`, `time?`, `tone?`, `status?`, `width?`.
- `KeyValueList`: `rows: KeyValueRow[]`, `c`, `title?`, `width?`, `minWidth?`, `keyWidth?`, `gap?: number = 0`, `fontSize?: number = 11`, `divider?: boolean = true`, `keyMono?: boolean = false`, `math?: boolean = false`. `KeyValueRow`: `key`, `value`, `tone?`, `valueMono?`.
- `Comparison`: `sides: ComparisonSideSpec[]`, `c`, `divider?: ReactNode | boolean = false`, `gap?: number = 14`, `sideWidth?`, `minHeight?`, `align?: FlexAlign = "stretch"`, `math?: boolean = false`. `ComparisonSideSpec`: `title`, `subtitle?`, `eyebrow?`, `tone?`, `lines?`, `children?`, `footer?`, `width?`.
- `DataTable`: `rows: ReactNode[][]`, `c`, `cellWidth?: number = 54`, `firstColWidth?: number = cellWidth`, `cellHeight?: number = 28`, `gap?: number = 5`, `headerRows?: number = 1`, `headerCols?: number = 1`, `fontSize?: number = 11`, `math?: boolean = false`.
- `Grid`: `rows: Array<Array<ReactNode | GridCell>>`, `c`, `cellWidth?: number = 34`, `cellHeight?: number = 30`, `gap?: number = 5`, `radius?: number = 7`, `fontSize?: number = 11`, `math?: boolean = false`, `headerRows?: number = 0`, `headerCols?: number = 0`. `GridCell`: `label?`, `tone?`, `color?`, `backgroundColor?`, `borderColor?`, `opacity?`.
- `CodeBlock`: `lines: Array<ReactNode | CodeLineSpec>`, `c`, `title?`, `tone?`, `width?`, `minWidth?`, `fontSize?: number = 12`, `showLineNumbers?: boolean = false`, `padding?: number | string = 14`, `radius?: number = 10`, `background?`, `shadow?: boolean = false`, `math?: boolean = false`. `CodeLineSpec`: `text`, `tone?`, `dim?`, `prefix?`.

Tiles:

- `Tile`: combines `TileSpec` with display props. `TileSpec`: `title`, `subtitle?`, `eyebrow?`, `icon?`, `tone?`, `lines?`, `children?`, `width?`, `minHeight?`. Display props: `c`, `align?: "left" | "center" = "center"`, `padding?: number | string = "14px 16px"`, `radius?: number = 10`, `shadow?: boolean = true`, `math?: boolean = false`.
- `TileGrid`: `tiles: TileSpec[]`, `c`, `columns?`, `gap?: number = 12`, `tileWidth?`, `minHeight?`, `align?: "left" | "center" = "center"`, `math?: boolean = false`.

Flows and process diagrams:

- `Flow`: `stages: FlowStageSpec[]`, `c`, `direction?: "horizontal" | "vertical" = "horizontal"`, `gap?: number = 10`, `connectorLength?: number = 28`, `connectorTone?: ToneName = "neutral"`, `align?: FlexAlign = "center"`, `math?: boolean = false`. `FlowStageSpec`: `title`, `subtitle?`, `eyebrow?`, `tone?`, `lines?`, `children?`, `width?`, `minWidth?`, `minHeight?`, `padding?`.
- `FlowArrow`: `direction?: "down" | "right" | "up" | "left" = "right"`, `label?`, `length?: number = 40`, `c`, `tone?: ToneName = "blue"`, `color?`.
- `Connector`: same props as `FlowArrow`.
- `Pipeline`: `stages: PipelineStage[]`, `c`, `title?`. `PipelineStage`: `label`, `sublabel?`, `icon?`, `color?: ColorName`.

Graphs and networks:

- `LayeredNetwork`: `c`, `layers: LayeredNetworkLayer[]`, `activePath?: number[] = []`, `annotations?: string[] = []`, `formula?`, `legend?: string = "highlighted path"`, `width?: number = 900`, `height?: number = 400`, `nodeSize?: number = 56`, `showFormula?: boolean = true`. `LayeredNetworkLayer`: `title`, `nodes: string[]`, `tone?`.
- `GraphDiagram` routing options: `routing?: "dagre" | "straight" | "orthogonal" = "dagre"`, `routingClearance?: number = 12`. Dagre preserves existing routes; straight connects facing node sides; orthogonal avoids node boxes and group headers with right-angle paths. Node layout remains automatic or manual independently of routing. `GraphDiagramNode` additionally accepts `ports?: GraphDiagramPort[]`; a port is `{ id: string, side: "top" | "right" | "bottom" | "left", offset?: number = 0.5 }`. Offset is finite and in `[0, 1]`, running left to right or top to bottom. `GraphDiagramEdge` additionally accepts `fromPort?`, `toPort?`, `fromSide?`, and `toSide?`. An endpoint cannot combine a port reference with a side. Explicit anchors opt an edge into orthogonal geometry even in Dagre mode.
